title: Adaptive Immunity in Clinical Practice · Board-Ready

sources.title: CDC: Contraindications and Precautions to Vaccination
CDC: General Best Practices for Immunization

questions.question: A pregnant patient asks about receiving a live attenuated vaccine that is normally recommended outside pregnancy. Which principle should guide the decision?
choices: Live attenuated vaccines are generally avoided during pregnancy because of theoretical fetal risk; use the current product-specific guidance
All vaccines are contraindicated throughout pregnancy
Pregnancy increases the safety of every replicating vaccine
Administering half the usual live-vaccine dose removes fetal risk
rationales: CDC guidance generally avoids live attenuated vaccines during pregnancy while allowing indicated nonlive vaccines according to current recommendations.
Several nonlive vaccines may be recommended during pregnancy; pregnancy is not a contraindication to all vaccination.
Replicating vaccines are not made safer simply by pregnancy.
Dose reduction is not a validated method for removing the contraindication.
questions.explanation: Advanced vaccine decisions require identifying whether a product is live, checking pregnancy-specific guidance, and distinguishing a contraindication from a precaution.

questions.question: A child scheduled for routine immunization has mild rhinorrhea, normal activity, and no respiratory distress. The parent asks to postpone all vaccines. Which response best reflects immunization best practice?
choices: A mild acute illness is generally not a contraindication; screen for actual contraindications and vaccinate if otherwise appropriate
Any upper-respiratory symptom permanently contraindicates vaccination
Antibiotic use always requires restarting every vaccine series
A normal physical examination is legally required before every vaccine dose
rationales: Minor illness with or without low fever is commonly misperceived as a contraindication and should not automatically cause a missed opportunity.
Severity and specific contraindications matter; mild symptoms alone do not permanently preclude vaccination.
Antibiotic therapy usually does not invalidate prior doses or require restarting a series.
Providers should assess illness and contraindications, but a routine full examination is not a prerequisite for a well-appearing recipient.
questions.explanation: The decision distinguishes mild illness from moderate or severe acute illness, which is generally a precaution until improvement.

questions.question: A patient experienced documented anaphylaxis after a previous dose of a vaccine. What is the most accurate next step before any additional dose of that same vaccine?
choices: Treat the prior severe allergic reaction as a contraindication and obtain product-specific expert guidance
Give the same vaccine without screening because reactions never recur
Use routine antihistamine premedication as proof the dose is safe
Classify the history as a minor precaution that can always be ignored
rationales: Anaphylaxis after a previous dose or to a component is generally a contraindication to further doses containing that component unless evaluated under appropriate expert guidance.
Re-exposure can cause another severe reaction.
Premedication does not eliminate anaphylaxis risk or replace evaluation.
A contraindication carries greater risk than a routine precaution and should not be ignored.
questions.explanation: Correct classification prevents both unsafe vaccination and unnecessary avoidance caused by vague, nonanaphylactic allergy histories.

questions.question: Minutes after an injection, a patient develops generalized urticaria, wheezing, hypotension, and vomiting. Which action is the priority?
choices: Administer intramuscular epinephrine promptly and activate emergency support
Wait for an antihistamine to work before treating hypotension
Give an oral glucocorticoid as the sole immediate therapy
Observe because type I hypersensitivity is always self-limited
rationales: The multisystem rapid reaction is anaphylaxis; intramuscular epinephrine is first-line while airway, breathing, circulation, and emergency care are addressed.
Antihistamines do not rapidly reverse airway edema or shock and must not delay epinephrine.
Glucocorticoids have delayed effects and are not first-line monotherapy.
Anaphylaxis can progress rapidly and is not safely managed by observation alone.
questions.explanation: Pattern recognition and treatment priority are more important than waiting for laboratory confirmation in suspected anaphylaxis.

questions.question: A patient develops anemia after starting a drug. Testing shows IgG bound to red-cell surface antigens with complement-mediated clearance. Which hypersensitivity mechanism is most consistent?
choices: Type II antibody-mediated cytotoxic hypersensitivity
Type I IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity
Type III circulating immune-complex deposition
Type IV delayed T-cell-mediated hypersensitivity
rationales: Type II reactions involve IgG or IgM directed at cell-surface or matrix antigens, leading to destruction or altered function.
Type I reactions involve IgE, mast cells, and rapid mediator release.
Type III reactions involve deposited soluble antigen-antibody complexes.
Type IV reactions are mediated primarily by sensitized T cells rather than cell-bound antibody.
questions.explanation: Linking the target location and effector mechanism is more reliable than memorizing disease lists.

questions.question: A patient with systemic autoimmune disease develops hematuria and proteinuria. Biopsy shows granular immunoglobulin and complement deposition in glomeruli. Which mechanism best explains the injury?
choices: Type III immune-complex deposition activates complement and recruits inflammation
Type I mast-cell degranulation confined to the glomerulus
Type II antibody stimulation of a normal hormone receptor
Type IV contact hypersensitivity to urinary proteins
rationales: Deposited antigen-antibody complexes can activate complement and inflammatory cells, producing a granular pattern and tissue injury.
IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity does not explain granular immune deposits.
Receptor stimulation is a type II functional mechanism but is not the described glomerular process.
Contact hypersensitivity is T-cell mediated and not caused by urinary-protein contact.
questions.explanation: Immune-complex disease often affects filtration sites and small vessels where complexes deposit and activate complement.

questions.question: Forty-eight hours after wearing a nickel-containing watchband, a patient develops an intensely pruritic eczematous rash limited to the contact area. Which mechanism is most likely?
choices: Type IV delayed hypersensitivity mediated by sensitized T cells
Type I systemic IgE-mediated anaphylaxis
Type II antibody-mediated platelet destruction
Type III immune-complex vasculitis
rationales: Allergic contact dermatitis is a delayed T-cell-mediated response that commonly peaks after 24–72 hours.
The delayed localized dermatitis is not the rapid multisystem pattern of anaphylaxis.
Platelet-directed antibodies would cause thrombocytopenia rather than contact dermatitis.
Immune-complex vasculitis would have a different distribution and mechanism.
questions.explanation: Timing, distribution, and effector mechanism together identify delayed contact hypersensitivity.

questions.question: Before initiating a potent tumor-necrosis-factor inhibitor for inflammatory disease, why is evaluation for latent tuberculosis important?
choices: TNF signaling helps maintain granuloma containment, so inhibition can permit reactivation
The medication increases terminal complement pores that destroy lung tissue
TNF inhibition permanently raises vaccine antibody titers
Latent tuberculosis is an IgE-mediated allergy to mycobacterial protein
rationales: TNF contributes to macrophage activation and granuloma integrity; blocking it can impair containment of latent mycobacteria.
The primary concern is cellular immune containment, not excess terminal complement.
TNF inhibitors are immunosuppressive and do not reliably enhance vaccine responses.
Latent infection is not an IgE allergy.
questions.explanation: Immunomodulators create pathway-specific infection risks, so preventive screening should be linked to the drug's mechanism.

questions.question: An adult has recurrent bacterial sinus and lung infections, low IgG and IgA, and poor response to protein vaccines; T-cell numbers are near normal. Which defect is most likely?
choices: A predominantly humoral immunodeficiency with impaired antibody production
Isolated terminal complement deficiency
Severe congenital neutropenia
Excessive natural-killer-cell cytotoxicity
rationales: Recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infection plus low immunoglobulins and poor vaccine response points to impaired humoral immunity.
Terminal complement deficiency more strongly suggests recurrent Neisseria and does not cause broadly low immunoglobulins.
Severe neutropenia would be evident on cell counts and has a different infection pattern.
Excess NK activity does not explain low IgG and IgA.
questions.explanation: Quantitative immunoglobulins plus functional vaccine responses help evaluate suspected antibody deficiency.

questions.question: An older adult receiving substantial immunosuppressive therapy asks which vaccines are safe. What is the best general approach?
choices: Review the current schedule and product type; avoid live vaccines in severe immunosuppression while using indicated nonlive vaccines as recommended
Avoid every vaccine because nonlive vaccines can replicate uncontrollably
Give live vaccines at double dose to overcome reduced response
Rely only on remote childhood records because recommendations never change
rationales: Severe immunosuppression is generally a contraindication to live vaccines, while indicated nonlive vaccines may still be used under current guidance.
Nonlive vaccines cannot replicate in the manner implied.
Increasing a live-vaccine dose is unsafe and not recommended.
Age, risk, therapy, and schedules change; current records and recommendations must be reviewed.
questions.explanation: The safe decision is product- and host-specific rather than a blanket yes or no to all immunization.
